title: Active Voice
description: Using active voice for clear, direct writing
content:
In active voice, the subject performs the action: 'The researcher conducted the study.' Active voice is generally clearer and more direct than passive voice, making it preferred in most academic writing.

Active voice helps readers immediately understand who is doing what. It creates more engaging, easier-to-follow sentences.

examples.label: Active Voice
examples.text: The student wrote the essay.

examples.label: Passive Voice
examples.text: The essay was written by the student.

examples.label: Active Voice
examples.text: Researchers discovered a new species.

examples.label: Passive Voice
examples.text: A new species was discovered by researchers.

resources.title: Purdue OWL: Active vs. Passive Voice

questions.question: Which sentence uses active voice?
sentences: The ball was thrown by Maria.
The results were analyzed by the team.
questions.explanation: 'Maria threw the ball' is active voice—the subject (Maria) performs the action (threw).

questions.question: Convert to active voice: 'The book was read by thousands of students.'
options: The book read thousands of students.
Thousands of students read the book.
The book was reading thousands of students.
Reading the book was thousands of students.
questions.answer: Thousands of students read the book.
questions.explanation: In active voice, the subject (thousands of students) performs the action (read) on the object (the book).

questions.question: Active voice is always better than passive voice in academic writing.
questions.explanation: False. While active voice is often clearer, passive voice has appropriate uses, such as when the action is more important than who performed it, or when the performer is unknown.

title: Adjectives
description: Understanding adjectives: words that describe nouns
content:
Adjectives describe or modify nouns and pronouns. They answer questions like: Which one? What kind? How many?

Types of Adjectives:

  • Descriptive: Describe qualities (blue, tall, happy, ancient)
  • Quantitative: Tell how many or how much (three, many, some)
  • Demonstrative: Point out specific things (this, that, these, those)
  • Articles: A, an, the

Degrees of Comparison:

  • Positive: Base form (tall, beautiful)
  • Comparative: Compares two (taller, more beautiful)
  • Superlative: Compares three or more (tallest, most beautiful)

Adjectives usually come before the noun they modify, but can come after linking verbs.

examples.label: Before Noun
examples.text: The red car drove quickly.

examples.label: After Linking Verb
examples.text: The car is red.

examples.label: Comparative
examples.text: She is taller than her brother.

examples.label: Superlative
examples.text: He is the tallest player on the team.

questions.question: Which word is an adjective?
questions.explanation: 'Beautiful' describes a noun, making it an adjective. The others are adverbs or verbs.

questions.question: What is the superlative form of 'good'?
questions.explanation: 'Good' has an irregular superlative: good → better → best.

questions.question: Which sentence uses an adjective correctly?
questions.explanation: 'Careful' is an adjective describing the noun 'driver.'

questions.question: Adjectives can only come before nouns.
questions.explanation: False. Adjectives can also come after linking verbs (The sky is blue).

title: Adverbs
description: Understanding adverbs: words that modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs
content:
Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. They answer: How? When? Where? To what extent?

What Adverbs Modify:

  • Verbs: She ran quickly. (How did she run?)
  • Adjectives: The very tall building (How tall?)
  • Other Adverbs: He runs extremely fast. (How fast?)

Types of Adverbs:

  • Manner (how): quickly, carefully, well
  • Time (when): now, yesterday, soon, always
  • Place (where): here, there, everywhere
  • Degree (to what extent): very, too, quite, extremely
  • Frequency (how often): always, never, often, seldom

Many adverbs end in -ly, but not all (fast, well, very).

examples.label: Modifying Verb
examples.text: She speaks softly.

examples.label: Modifying Adjective
examples.text: The extremely cold weather surprised us.

examples.label: Modifying Adverb
examples.text: He works very diligently.

examples.label: Different Types
examples.text: She often (frequency) arrives early (time) and works efficiently (manner) there (place).

resources.title: Schoolhouse Rock: Lolly, Lolly, Lolly, Get Your Adverbs Here

questions.question: Which word is an adverb?
questions.explanation: 'Happily' is an adverb (ends in -ly) that describes how an action is done.

questions.question: What does the adverb modify in: 'The very tall tree'?
questions.explanation: 'Very' modifies the adjective 'tall' (how tall?).

questions.question: Which sentence uses an adverb correctly?
questions.explanation: 'Quickly' is an adverb modifying the verb 'worked.'

questions.question: All words ending in -ly are adverbs.
questions.explanation: False. Some adjectives end in -ly (friendly, lovely, lonely).

title: Affect vs. Effect
description: Understanding when to use affect (verb) vs. effect (noun)
content:
These words are commonly confused because they sound similar and are related in meaning.

Affect (verb) = to influence or change something
Effect (noun) = the result or consequence of something

Memory trick: Affect is an Action (verb). Effect is the End result (noun).

examples.label: Affect (Verb)
examples.text: The weather will affect our plans.

examples.label: Effect (Noun)
examples.text: The new law had a positive effect on the community.

examples.label: Common Mistake
examples.text: Incorrect: The rain will effect the game. → Correct: The rain will affect the game.

examples.label: Note
examples.text: Occasionally 'effect' can be a verb meaning 'to bring about' (effect change), but this is less common.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'How will this decision ___ the students?'
questions.explanation: Use 'affect' (verb) because the decision will influence/change something for the students.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The study examined the ___ of sleep on performance.'
questions.explanation: Use 'effect' (noun) because we're talking about the result or impact of sleep.

questions.question: Which sentence is correct?
sentences: The medicine had no affect on my symptoms.
Poor nutrition can effect your health.
The changes will effect everyone in the office.
questions.explanation: 'Climate change affects global temperatures' correctly uses 'affects' as a verb.

questions.question: Affect is usually a verb, and effect is usually a noun.
questions.explanation: True. While there are exceptions, this is the most common usage pattern.

title: Annotated Works Cited
description: Creating an annotated bibliography in MLA format
content:
An annotated bibliography (or annotated Works Cited page) includes the citation for each source followed by a brief annotation—a paragraph that summarizes, evaluates, and/or reflects on the source. Annotations help you think critically about your sources and explain their relevance to your research.

A typical annotation includes: (1) a summary of the source's main argument or content, (2) an evaluation of the source's credibility and usefulness, and (3) a reflection on how the source fits into your research.

Annotations are usually 150-200 words and appear immediately after each citation entry.

examples.label: Full Annotated Entry
examples.text:
Smith, John. Climate Change and Society. Oxford UP, 2020.

     This book examines the social and economic impacts of climate change on communities worldwide. Smith argues that addressing climate change requires not only scientific solutions but also social policy reforms. The book is well-researched, drawing on data from multiple countries and disciplines. As a professor of environmental sociology, Smith brings credibility to his analysis. This source is useful for my research on community responses to climate change because it provides a framework for understanding how social structures affect environmental outcomes. The chapter on urban adaptation strategies will be particularly relevant to my argument.

questions.question: An annotation should only summarize the source's content.
questions.explanation: False. A good annotation summarizes, evaluates, and reflects on the source's relevance to your research.

questions.question: What should appear first in an annotated bibliography entry?
questions.explanation: The complete MLA citation comes first, followed by the annotation paragraph.

questions.question: What is the typical length of an annotation?
questions.explanation: Most annotations are about 150-200 words—long enough to summarize, evaluate, and reflect meaningfully.

questions.question: Annotations should be written in the same tone as the source you're annotating.
questions.explanation: False. Annotations should be written in your own voice, summarizing and evaluating the source objectively.

title: APA Document Formatting
description: Formatting your technical writing paper in APA style
content:
APA format provides specific guidelines for formatting academic and technical papers, including margins, fonts, headers, and title pages.

Key formatting requirements:
- 1-inch margins on all sides
- 12-point Times New Roman or similar font
- Double-space throughout entire paper
- Running head in header (page number on right)
- Title page with title, author, affiliation
- Separate Abstract page if required

examples.label: Title Page Elements
examples.text:
Title of Paper (bold, centered)
Your Name
Your School/Institution
Course Name
Instructor Name
Due Date

examples.label: Running Head
examples.text: Page number appears in top right corner of every page

examples.label: Section Headings
examples.text:
Level 1: Centered, Bold, Title Case
Level 2: Left-aligned, Bold, Title Case
Level 3: Left-aligned, Bold Italic, Title Case

questions.question: What font size should be used in APA format?
questions.explanation: APA requires 12-point font, typically Times New Roman or similar serif font.

questions.question: What margin size is required in APA format?
questions.explanation: APA format requires 1-inch margins on all sides of the page.

questions.question: APA papers should be double-spaced throughout.
questions.explanation: True. The entire paper, including title page, references, and all text, should be double-spaced.

questions.question: Where does the page number appear in APA format?
questions.explanation: Page numbers appear in the top right corner of the header on every page.

title: APA In-Text Citations
description: Citing sources within your text using APA format
content:
In-text citations in APA format give credit to sources you use in your writing. They appear in parentheses within your text and correspond to entries on your References page.

Basic format: (Author's Last Name, Year)
Example: (Johnson, 2020)

Key rules:
- Include author's last name and publication year
- Use comma between name and year
- For direct quotes, add page number: (Johnson, 2020, p. 15)
- For multiple authors, use '&' not 'and'
- Place citation before period at end of sentence

examples.label: Basic Citation
examples.text: Recent research shows climate patterns are changing (Johnson, 2020).

examples.label: Author Named in Sentence
examples.text: Johnson (2020) argues that climate patterns are changing.

examples.label: Direct Quote
examples.text: According to Johnson (2020), "climate patterns have shifted dramatically" (p. 15).

examples.label: Two Authors
examples.text: The study found significant results (Smith & Jones, 2019).

examples.label: Three or More Authors
examples.text: Multiple factors contribute to this trend (Williams et al., 2021).

questions.question: Which in-text citation is formatted correctly in APA?
questions.explanation: APA format uses author's last name, comma, and year in parentheses.

questions.question: How do you cite a direct quote with a page number in APA?
questions.explanation: For direct quotes, include author, year, and page number with 'p.' before the number.

questions.question: In APA, use 'and' between two authors in parenthetical citations.
questions.explanation: False. APA uses '&' (ampersand) between authors in parenthetical citations: (Smith & Jones, 2020).

questions.question: How do you cite a work with three or more authors in APA?
options: Use first author's name followed by 'et al.'
Use first two authors and 'et al.'
questions.answer: Use first author's name followed by 'et al.'
questions.explanation: For three or more authors, use the first author's name followed by 'et al.': (Williams et al., 2021).

title: APA References Page
description: Creating a properly formatted References page in APA style
content:
The References page lists all sources cited in your paper. It appears on a separate page at the end of your document.

Key formatting rules:
- Title: 'References' (centered, bold)
- Alphabetize entries by author's last name
- Use hanging indent (first line flush left, subsequent lines indented)
- Double-space everything
- Include: Author, A. A. (Year). Title of work. Publisher.

examples.label: Book
examples.text: Smith, J. D. (2020). The art of technical writing. Oxford University Press.

examples.label: Journal Article
examples.text: Brown, S. L., & Miller, T. K. (2019). Effective communication strategies. Journal of Technical Communication, 45(2), 112-125. https://doi.org/10.xxxx

examples.label: Website
examples.text: Jones, M. (2021, March 15). Digital literacy in education. Education Today. https://www.edtoday.com/digital-literacy

examples.label: Hanging Indent Visual
examples.text:
First line starts here
     Second line indented
     Third line indented

questions.question: What is the correct title for the reference page in APA format?
questions.explanation: APA format uses 'References' as the title, centered and bold.

questions.question: APA References entries should be in alphabetical order.
questions.explanation: True. Entries are alphabetized by the first author's last name.

questions.question: What type of indentation is used for APA References entries?
questions.explanation: Use a hanging indent: first line flush left, subsequent lines indented 0.5 inches.

questions.question: In APA, the References page title should be bold.
questions.explanation: True. The word 'References' should be centered and bold at the top of the page.

title: Apostrophes
description: Using apostrophes for possession and contractions
content:
Apostrophes have two main uses: showing possession (ownership) and forming contractions (combining words). Knowing when and where to use apostrophes prevents common errors.

For possession: Add 's to singular nouns (the student's book) and just an apostrophe after plural nouns ending in s (the students' books). For contractions: The apostrophe replaces missing letters (don't = do not).

examples.label: Singular Possessive
examples.text: The teacher's desk is organized.

examples.label: Plural Possessive
examples.text: The teachers' lounge is on the second floor.

examples.label: Contraction
examples.text: It's (it is) a beautiful day.

examples.label: Possessive Pronoun (NO apostrophe)
examples.text: The dog wagged its tail.

questions.question: Which sentence uses apostrophes correctly?
questions.explanation: For a singular possessive (one cat owns the toy), add 's to the noun.

questions.question: Which is correct?
questions.explanation: It's = it is (contraction). Its = possessive form (no apostrophe).

questions.question: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: 'The dog's bowl' shows that the bowl belongs to the dog (singular possessive).

title: Author, Narrator, and Character
description: Understanding the distinctions between author, narrator, and character
content:
In literary analysis, it's crucial to distinguish between the author (the person who wrote the work), the narrator (the voice telling the story), and the characters (the people in the story).

Author: The real person who created the work
Narrator: The voice or persona telling the story (may be a character or outside observer)
Character: A person, animal, or entity within the story

Important: Never assume the narrator represents the author's personal views. The narrator is a literary creation, separate from the author.

examples.label: Incorrect
examples.text: In 'The Cask of Amontillado,' Edgar Allan Poe seeks revenge on Fortunato.

examples.label: Correct
examples.text: In 'The Cask of Amontillado,' the narrator Montresor seeks revenge on Fortunato.

examples.label: Incorrect
examples.text: In 'The Yellow Wallpaper,' Charlotte Perkins Gilman is trapped in a room.

examples.label: Correct
examples.text: In 'The Yellow Wallpaper,' the narrator (an unnamed woman) is trapped in a room by her husband John.

questions.question: The narrator and the author are always the same person.
questions.explanation: False. The narrator is a literary device created by the author, but they are distinct. The narrator is the voice telling the story, not necessarily the author's voice.

questions.question: In analyzing 'The Tell-Tale Heart,' who is experiencing guilt?
questions.explanation: The narrator (the unnamed person telling the story) experiences guilt, not Poe the author.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly distinguishes author from narrator?
sentences: In the poem, Robert Frost stops by woods on a snowy evening.
In the poem, Emily Dickinson hears a fly buzz when she died.
In the poem, the speaker stops by woods on a snowy evening.
In the story, Hemingway sits at a café in Paris.
questions.explanation: Correct! 'The speaker' (or 'the narrator') is the voice in the poem, distinct from Robert Frost the author.

title: Avoiding Second Person
description: Understanding when to avoid 'you' in academic writing
content:
Most academic writing avoids second person (you, your) because it's too informal and makes assumptions about the reader. Instead, use third person or occasionally first person.

Exceptions: Some disciplines and writing contexts do use 'you,' particularly in instructional writing or when directly addressing readers. Know your audience and assignment requirements.

examples.label: Second Person (Avoid)
examples.text: When you read this poem, you can see the symbolism.

examples.label: Third Person (Better)
examples.text: Readers can identify the symbolism throughout the poem.

examples.label: Second Person (Avoid)
examples.text: You should consider multiple perspectives when analyzing data.

examples.label: Third Person (Better)
examples.text: Researchers should consider multiple perspectives when analyzing data.

resources.title: UNC Writing Center: Point of View
Purdue OWL: Appropriate Point of View

questions.question: Which sentence avoids second person?
options: You can see that the author uses metaphor.
One can see that the author uses metaphor.
When you look closely, you see metaphor.
questions.answer: One can see that the author uses metaphor.
questions.explanation: Using 'one' or reconstructing to avoid direct address maintains academic formality.

questions.question: Second person (you) is never acceptable in any type of academic writing.
questions.explanation: False. Some writing contexts, like instructional guides or reflective pieces, may appropriately use second person.

title: Avoiding Wordiness
description: Writing concisely and eliminating unnecessary words
content:
Wordiness occurs when you use more words than necessary to express an idea. Academic writing values clarity and precision, which often means using fewer, more precise words.

Common sources of wordiness: redundant phrases, passive voice, excessive nominalizations (turning verbs into nouns), and filler words. Aim to express ideas as directly as possible.

examples.label: Wordy
examples.text: Due to the fact that it was raining, we decided to stay home.

examples.label: Concise
examples.text: Because it was raining, we stayed home.

examples.label: Wordy
examples.text: In my personal opinion, I think that the study is very interesting.

examples.label: Concise
examples.text: The study is interesting.

examples.label: Wordy
examples.text: The reason why she left is because she was tired.

examples.label: Concise
examples.text: She left because she was tired.

questions.question: Which is the most concise version?
options: At this point in time, we are currently working on the project.
Currently at this point in time we work on the project.
We are currently working on the project.
At this point we are working on the project currently.
questions.answer: We are currently working on the project.
questions.explanation: This version eliminates redundant phrases like 'at this point in time' while maintaining clarity.

questions.question: Which phrase is redundant?
questions.explanation: 'Finished' already means complete, so 'completely finished' is redundant.

title: Capitalization
description: Understanding capitalization rules in academic writing
content:
Capitalization rules help distinguish proper nouns (specific names) from common nouns (general things). In academic writing, consistent capitalization is important for clarity.

Capitalize: 1) First word of a sentence, 2) Proper nouns (specific names of people, places, organizations), 3) Major words in titles, 4) The pronoun 'I'. Don't capitalize: common nouns, seasons (unless part of a proper name), family relationships used generally.

examples.label: Correct
examples.text: I visited New York City with my mother last spring.

examples.label: Incorrect
examples.text: I visited new york city with my Mother last Spring.

examples.label: Correct
examples.text: My English professor assigned a book.

examples.label: Correct
examples.text: I spoke with Professor Martinez.

questions.question: Which sentence has correct capitalization?
options: I saw my Uncle at the store.
I saw my uncle at the Store.
I saw my uncle at the store.
i saw my Uncle at the Store.
questions.answer: I saw my uncle at the store.
questions.explanation: 'Uncle' and 'store' are common nouns here, not proper names, so they shouldn't be capitalized.

questions.question: Seasons (spring, summer, fall, winter) should always be capitalized.
questions.explanation: False. Seasons are only capitalized when they're part of a proper name, like 'Spring Festival' or 'Winter Olympics.'

title: Colons
description: Using colons to introduce lists and explanations
content:
Colons introduce lists, explanations, or elaborations. What comes before the colon should be a complete sentence (independent clause).

Common uses: 1) Introducing a list, 2) Introducing an explanation or example, 3) Introducing a quote (in some cases). The key rule: the part before the colon must be able to stand alone as a complete sentence.

examples.label: Introducing a List
examples.text: You'll need three things: patience, practice, and persistence.

examples.label: Introducing Explanation
examples.text: The decision was clear: we had to move forward.

examples.label: Incorrect
examples.text: The ingredients are: flour, sugar, and eggs.

examples.label: Correct
examples.text: The ingredients are flour, sugar, and eggs.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
options: I need: bread, milk, and eggs.
I need the following items: bread, milk, and eggs.
I: need bread, milk, and eggs.
I need bread: milk, and eggs.
questions.answer: I need the following items: bread, milk, and eggs.
questions.explanation: The part before the colon ('I need the following items') is a complete sentence, which is required.

questions.question: What comes before a colon must be a complete sentence.
questions.explanation: True. The clause before a colon should be able to stand alone as a complete sentence.

title: Comma Splices
description: Understanding and fixing comma splice errors
content:
A comma splice occurs when two independent clauses are joined with only a comma, without a coordinating conjunction. This is one of the most common errors in student writing.

There are several ways to fix a comma splice: use a period to make two sentences, add a coordinating conjunction after the comma, use a semicolon, or make one clause dependent on the other.

examples.label: Comma Splice
examples.text: The exam was difficult, I studied for hours.

examples.label: Fixed with Period
examples.text: The exam was difficult. I studied for hours.

examples.label: Fixed with Conjunction
examples.text: The exam was difficult, so I studied for hours.

examples.label: Fixed with Semicolon
examples.text: The exam was difficult; I studied for hours.

questions.question: Which sentence contains a comma splice?
sentences: I wanted to go, but I was too tired.
She likes coffee, he prefers tea.
After the movie ended, we went home.
questions.explanation: 'She likes coffee, he prefers tea' joins two independent clauses with only a comma—that's a comma splice.

questions.question: Which coordinating conjunction could fix this comma splice: 'I was hungry, I made a sandwich'?
questions.explanation: 'So' is a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) that can follow a comma to join independent clauses. The others are subordinating conjunctions.

questions.question: Semicolons can be used to fix comma splices.
questions.explanation: True. A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses, making it one way to fix a comma splice.

title: Comma Usage
description: Using commas correctly in various situations
content:
Commas serve many purposes: separating items in a list, joining independent clauses with conjunctions, setting off introductory elements, and more. Learning the main comma rules helps make your writing clearer.

Key uses: 1) After introductory elements, 2) Before coordinating conjunctions joining independent clauses, 3) Between items in a series, 4) Around non-essential information, 5) Between coordinate adjectives.

examples.label: After Introductory Element
examples.text: After the concert ended, we went home.

examples.label: With Conjunction
examples.text: I wanted to go, but I was too tired.

examples.label: Series
examples.text: We need eggs, milk, bread, and butter.

examples.label: Non-essential Info
examples.text: My sister, who lives in Boston, is visiting.

questions.question: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
options: After we ate we went home.
After we ate, we went home.
After, we ate we went home.
After we, ate we went home.
questions.answer: After we ate, we went home.
questions.explanation: Use a comma after an introductory clause (After we ate).

questions.question: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
sentences: I bought apples oranges and bananas.
I bought apples, oranges and, bananas.
I bought apples, oranges, and bananas.
I bought, apples oranges and bananas.
questions.explanation: Items in a series should be separated by commas, with a comma before 'and' (Oxford comma) for clarity.

questions.question: You should use a comma before 'and' when it joins two independent clauses.
questions.explanation: True. When 'and' joins two independent clauses (complete sentences), use a comma before it.

title: Conjunctions
description: Understanding conjunctions: words that connect
content:
Conjunctions connect words, phrases, or clauses. There are three types of conjunctions.

1. Coordinating Conjunctions (FANBOYS):

Connect equal grammatical elements (words, phrases, independent clauses).

  • F - For
  • A - And
  • N - Nor
  • B - But
  • O - Or
  • Y - Yet
  • S - So

2. Subordinating Conjunctions:

Connect a dependent clause to an independent clause: because, although, since, while, if, when, until, before, after, unless, whereas, as

3. Correlative Conjunctions:

Work in pairs to connect equal elements: either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also, whether...or

examples.label: Coordinating
examples.text: I want pizza, but she wants tacos.

examples.label: Subordinating
examples.text: We stayed inside because it was raining.

examples.label: Correlative
examples.text: Either you go, or I will.

examples.label: Correlative (both...and)
examples.text: She is both intelligent and kind.

questions.question: Which is a coordinating conjunction?
questions.explanation: 'And' is a coordinating conjunction (part of FANBOYS).

questions.question: Which pair is correlative conjunctions?
questions.explanation: 'Either...or' is a pair of correlative conjunctions.

questions.question: Which is a subordinating conjunction?
questions.explanation: 'Because' is a subordinating conjunction that creates a dependent clause.

questions.question: FANBOYS stands for the seven coordinating conjunctions.
questions.explanation: True. FANBOYS = For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So.

title: Dangling Modifiers
description: Avoiding and fixing dangling modifiers
content:
A dangling modifier is a descriptive phrase that doesn't clearly connect to what it's supposed to describe. This happens when the word being modified is missing or too far from the modifier.

To fix: Make sure the word being described appears right after the modifier, or restructure the sentence to make the connection clear.

examples.label: Dangling
examples.text: Walking to class, the rain started falling.

examples.label: Corrected
examples.text: Walking to class, I noticed the rain started falling.

examples.label: Dangling
examples.text: After studying all night, the test was easy.

examples.label: Corrected
examples.text: After studying all night, I found the test easy.

questions.question: Which sentence has a dangling modifier?
sentences: After finishing my homework, I watched TV.
Running late, the bus had already left.
Before leaving, we locked the door.
questions.explanation: 'Running late' modifies 'the bus,' but buses don't run late—people do. It should be: 'Because I was running late, the bus had already left.'

questions.question: How can you fix: 'Covered in frosting, we ate the cake'?
options: Covered in frosting, the cake we ate.
We ate the cake covered in frosting.
Covered in frosting, eating the cake.
We covered in frosting ate the cake.
questions.answer: We ate the cake covered in frosting.
questions.explanation: Moving 'covered in frosting' next to 'cake' makes it clear that the cake (not we) was covered in frosting.

title: Formal Academic Tone
description: Maintaining appropriate tone in academic writing
content:
Academic writing typically uses a formal tone that's clear, objective, and professional. This doesn't mean being stuffy or using complicated words—it means being precise and respectful of your subject and audience.

Key elements: avoid contractions, minimize first/second person (I/you) in most academic writing, use precise vocabulary, avoid slang and colloquialisms, maintain objectivity.

examples.label: Too Informal
examples.text: The experiment was super cool and it totally proved the hypothesis.

examples.label: Formal
examples.text: The experiment successfully demonstrated the validity of the hypothesis.

examples.label: Too Informal
examples.text: A lot of people think that social media is bad for you.

examples.label: Formal
examples.text: Research suggests that excessive social media use correlates with negative mental health outcomes.

questions.question: Which sentence has an appropriate academic tone?
options: The results were pretty awesome and showed we were right.
We were totally right about what would happen.
questions.explanation: This version is clear, precise, and maintains professional tone without informal language.

questions.question: Contractions (like can't, won't, it's) should generally be avoided in formal academic writing.
questions.explanation: True. While contractions are fine in informal writing, academic writing typically avoids them for a more formal tone.

title: Interjections
description: Understanding interjections: words that express emotion
content:
Interjections are words or phrases that express sudden emotion or feeling. They stand alone and are not grammatically connected to the rest of the sentence.

Common Interjections:

  • Surprise: Wow! Oh! Gosh!
  • Pain: Ouch! Ow!
  • Greeting: Hey! Hi! Hello!
  • Joy: Yay! Hooray! Woohoo!
  • Disapproval: Ugh! Yuck!
  • Hesitation: Um, uh, well
  • Sadness: Alas! Oh no!

Interjections are usually followed by an exclamation point for strong emotion, or a comma for mild emotion.

Note: Interjections are uncommon in formal academic writing.

examples.label: Strong Emotion
examples.text: Wow! That's amazing!

examples.label: Mild Emotion
examples.text: Well, I suppose we could try.

examples.label: Standalone
examples.text: Ouch! That hurt.

examples.label: Multiple
examples.text: Oh! Hey! I didn't see you there.

questions.question: Which is an interjection?
questions.explanation: 'Wow' is an interjection expressing surprise or amazement.

questions.question: How should a strong interjection be punctuated?
questions.explanation: Strong interjections are followed by an exclamation point.

questions.question: Which word is an interjection?
questions.explanation: 'Oh' is an interjection expressing sudden realization.

questions.question: Interjections are commonly used in formal academic writing.
questions.explanation: False. Interjections express emotion and are generally avoided in formal academic writing.

title: Its vs. It's
description: Understanding the difference between its (possessive) and it's (contraction)
content:
This is one of the most common errors in student writing. The confusion comes from mixing up possessive forms and contractions.

It's = contraction meaning "it is" or "it has"
Its = possessive pronoun meaning "belonging to it"

Tip: If you can replace the word with "it is" or "it has," use it's. If not, use its.

examples.label: Correct (Contraction)
examples.text: It's raining outside. (It is raining)

examples.label: Correct (Possessive)
examples.text: The dog wagged its tail.

examples.label: Incorrect
examples.text: The car lost it's wheel.

examples.label: Correct
examples.text: The car lost its wheel.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The company announced ___ new policy.'
questions.explanation: Use 'its' (possessive) because the policy belongs to the company. You can't substitute 'it is' here.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: '___ been a long day.'
questions.explanation: Use 'it's' because it's a contraction of 'it has.' Both 'It's' and 'It has' work here.

questions.question: Which sentence is correct?
sentences: The book has its pages torn.
questions.explanation: 'The book has its pages torn' correctly uses 'its' as possessive.

questions.question: The word 'its'' (with an apostrophe at the end) is a valid word.
questions.explanation: False. There is no such word as 'its'.' Use 'its' for possessive or 'it's' for contraction.

title: Literary Present Tense
description: Using present tense when writing about literature and art
content:
When writing about literature, art, or film, use present tense to discuss events, themes, and elements within the work. This convention treats the work as existing in an eternal 'now.'

Even if the story was written long ago or uses past tense narration, discuss it in present tense. The characters' actions, the author's techniques, and the work's themes all exist perpetually in the present when we read or view them.

examples.label: Incorrect (Past Tense)
examples.text: In 'Romeo and Juliet,' the two lovers died at the end.

examples.label: Correct (Present Tense)
examples.text: In 'Romeo and Juliet,' the two lovers die at the end.

examples.label: Incorrect
examples.text: Hamlet struggled with the decision to avenge his father.

examples.label: Correct
examples.text: Hamlet struggles with the decision to avenge his father.

examples.label: Correct (Author's techniques)
examples.text: Shakespeare uses dramatic irony to heighten tension in Act III.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses literary present tense?
options: In the novel, Atticus defended Tom Robinson.
In the novel, Atticus defends Tom Robinson.
In the novel, Atticus will defend Tom Robinson.
In the novel, Atticus had defended Tom Robinson.
questions.answer: In the novel, Atticus defends Tom Robinson.
questions.explanation: Use present tense when discussing events in literature: 'defends' not 'defended.'

questions.question: You should use past tense when writing about a novel written in the 19th century.
questions.explanation: False. Always use present tense when discussing literature, regardless of when it was written.

questions.question: Which sentence uses correct literary present tense?
sentences: The narrator described the house as gloomy and dark.
The narrator describes the house as gloomy and dark.
The narrator will describe the house as gloomy and dark.
The narrator had described the house as gloomy and dark.
questions.explanation: 'The narrator describes' is correct—use present tense for actions in literature.

title: MLA In-Text Citations
description: Properly citing sources within your text using MLA format
content:
In-text citations give credit to sources you use in your writing. They appear in parentheses within your text and correspond to entries on your Works Cited page.

Basic format: (Author's Last Name Page Number)
Example: (Smith 42)

Key rules:
- No comma between name and page number
- No 'p.' or 'pg.' before page number
- Place citation before period at end of sentence
- If no author, use shortened title in quotes

examples.label: Basic Citation
examples.text: According to research, climate patterns are changing (Johnson 15).

examples.label: Author Named in Sentence
examples.text: Johnson argues that climate patterns are changing (15).

examples.label: No Author
examples.text: Recent studies show concerning trends ("Climate Report" 23).

examples.label: Two Authors
examples.text: The study found significant results (Smith and Jones 87).

questions.question: Which in-text citation is formatted correctly?
questions.explanation: MLA format uses author's last name and page number with no comma or abbreviation.

questions.question: Where should the in-text citation be placed?
options: Before the period at the end of the sentence
At the beginning of the paragraph
questions.answer: Before the period at the end of the sentence
questions.explanation: The citation goes before the final period: (Author Page).

questions.question: If the author's name appears in your sentence, you still need to include it in the parenthetical citation.
questions.explanation: False. If you mention the author in your sentence, only include the page number in parentheses.

questions.question: How do you cite a source with two authors?
questions.explanation: For two authors, use 'and' between the names: (Smith and Jones 45).

title: MLA Signal Phrases
description: Using signal phrases to introduce sources in MLA style
content:
Signal phrases introduce quotations, paraphrases, and summaries in your writing. They tell readers who said or wrote something and provide context for the source material. In MLA style, signal phrases typically include the author's name and a verb.

Common signal verbs: argues, asserts, claims, comments, contends, declares, explains, illustrates, notes, observes, points out, reports, states, suggests, writes.

Signal phrases help integrate sources smoothly into your writing and give proper credit to authors.

examples.label: Basic Signal Phrase
examples.text: According to Smith, "climate change requires immediate action" (45).

examples.label: Signal Phrase with Verb
examples.text: Johnson argues that "education reform must prioritize equity" (112).

examples.label: Mid-Sentence Signal
examples.text: "The data shows," Martinez explains, "a clear correlation between the variables" (78).

examples.label: Multiple Authors
examples.text: As Brown and Lee observe, "collaboration enhances learning outcomes" (234).

questions.question: Which signal phrase is most appropriate for MLA style?
options: The book says that "reading improves vocabulary."
According to the author, "reading improves vocabulary."
questions.explanation: MLA style uses the author's last name in the signal phrase and the page number in parentheses after the quote.

questions.question: You should use the same signal verb (like 'says') repeatedly throughout your paper.
questions.explanation: False. Varying your signal verbs makes your writing more engaging and can convey different relationships to the source material.

questions.question: Where should the page number appear in MLA format?
options: After the period at the end of the sentence
At the beginning of the sentence
questions.explanation: In MLA style, the page number appears in parentheses after the quote but before the final punctuation.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a signal phrase?
sentences: The article says "Education is important" on page 12.
questions.explanation: This correctly uses a signal phrase with the author's name, proper punctuation, and MLA citation format.

title: MLA Works Cited
description: Creating a properly formatted Works Cited page in MLA style
content:
The Works Cited page lists all sources you cited in your paper. It appears on a separate page at the end of your document.

Key formatting rules:
- Title: "Works Cited" (centered, not bold or italicized)
- Alphabetize entries by author's last name
- Use hanging indent (first line flush left, subsequent lines indented)
- Double-space everything
- Include: Author. Title. Container, other contributors, version, number, publisher, date, location.

examples.label: Book
examples.text: Smith, John. The Art of Writing. Oxford UP, 2020.

examples.label: Article from Website
examples.text: Jones, Mary. "Digital Literacy in Education." Education Today, 15 Mar. 2021, www.edtoday.com/digital-literacy.

examples.label: Journal Article
examples.text: Brown, Sarah. "Teaching Grammar Effectively." Journal of Education, vol. 45, no. 2, 2019, pp. 112-125.

examples.label: Hanging Indent Visual
examples.text:
[First line starts here]
     [Second line indented]
     [Third line indented]

resources.title: UNC Writing Center: MLA Works Cited

questions.question: What is the correct title for the reference page in MLA format?
questions.explanation: MLA format uses 'Works Cited' as the title for the reference page.

questions.question: Works Cited entries should be in alphabetical order by the author's last name.
questions.explanation: True. Entries are alphabetized by the first word in the entry, usually the author's last name.

questions.question: What type of indentation is used for Works Cited entries?
questions.explanation: Use a hanging indent: first line flush left, subsequent lines indented.

questions.question: The Works Cited page should be single-spaced to save space.
questions.explanation: False. Like the rest of your MLA paper, the Works Cited page should be double-spaced.

title: Nouns
description: Understanding nouns: person, place, thing, or idea
content:
A noun is a word that names a person, place, thing, or idea. Nouns are the subjects and objects of sentences.

Types of Nouns:

  • Proper Nouns: Specific names, always capitalized (Sarah, Boston, Harvard University)
  • Common Nouns: General names, not capitalized (girl, city, university)
  • Concrete Nouns: Things you can perceive with senses (table, music, flower)
  • Abstract Nouns: Ideas or concepts (freedom, love, courage)
  • Singular: One item (cat, book)
  • Plural: More than one (cats, books, children)
  • Countable: Can be counted (three apples, five books)
  • Uncountable: Cannot be counted individually (water, rice, information)

examples.label: Proper vs. Common
examples.text: The student (common) went to Harvard University (proper).

examples.label: Concrete vs. Abstract
examples.text: Her courage (abstract) helped her climb the mountain (concrete).

examples.label: Singular vs. Plural
examples.text: One child plays; three children play. (irregular plural)

examples.label: Countable vs. Uncountable
examples.text: I need three books (countable) and some information (uncountable).

resources.title: Schoolhouse Rock: A Noun is a Person, Place or Thing

questions.question: Which of these is a proper noun?
questions.explanation: 'Chicago' is a proper noun—a specific place name that must be capitalized.

questions.question: What type of noun is 'freedom'?
questions.explanation: 'Freedom' is an abstract noun—an idea or concept you cannot perceive with your senses.

questions.question: Which is an irregular plural?
questions.explanation: 'Children' is irregular (child → children), while the others follow regular plural patterns.

questions.question: All nouns can be counted individually.
questions.explanation: False. Uncountable nouns like 'water,' 'information,' and 'advice' cannot be counted individually.

title: Paragraph Development
description: Building well-developed, unified paragraphs
content:
A well-developed paragraph has a clear main idea (topic sentence), supporting evidence, analysis, and unity. Each sentence should relate to the paragraph's main point.

Think of paragraph structure as: Point (topic sentence) → Evidence (support your point) → Explanation (show how evidence supports your point) → Link (connect to thesis or transition to next idea).

examples.label: Underdeveloped
examples.text: Exercise is important for health. It helps people feel better. Everyone should exercise more.

examples.label: Well-Developed
examples.text: Regular exercise significantly improves mental health outcomes. A 2020 study published in the Journal of Health Psychology found that participants who engaged in 30 minutes of moderate exercise five times per week reported 40% fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression compared to sedentary individuals. This improvement occurs because physical activity stimulates the production of endorphins and reduces cortisol levels, creating a biological basis for improved mood. These findings suggest that incorporating regular exercise into daily routines can be as effective as some traditional interventions for managing mild to moderate mental health concerns.

questions.question: What should come after presenting evidence in a paragraph?
options: Analysis explaining how the evidence supports your point
questions.answer: Analysis explaining how the evidence supports your point
questions.explanation: After presenting evidence, you need to explain its significance and show how it supports your point—don't assume readers will make the connection themselves.

questions.question: A paragraph can discuss multiple unrelated ideas.
questions.explanation: False. Paragraphs should have unity—all sentences should relate to the main idea stated in the topic sentence.

title: Parallel Structure
description: Maintaining parallel structure in lists and comparisons
content:
Parallel structure means using the same grammatical form for items in a list or comparison. This creates rhythm and clarity in your writing.

When listing actions, ideas, or qualities, keep them in the same grammatical form. If you start with verbs, use all verbs. If you use nouns, use all nouns. This applies to lists, comparisons, and paired ideas.

examples.label: Not Parallel
examples.text: I like reading, to write, and going for walks.

examples.label: Parallel
examples.text: I like reading, writing, and walking.

examples.label: Not Parallel
examples.text: The job requires attention to detail, being organized, and you must communicate well.

examples.label: Parallel
examples.text: The job requires attention to detail, organization, and strong communication skills.

questions.question: Which sentence has correct parallel structure?
options: She enjoys hiking, to swim, and biking.
She enjoys hiking, swimming, and biking.
She enjoys hiking, swimming, and to bike.
She enjoys to hike, swimming, and biking.
questions.answer: She enjoys hiking, swimming, and biking.
questions.explanation: All three items use the -ing form (gerunds), maintaining parallel structure.

questions.question: Which sentence maintains parallel structure?
sentences: The teacher is kind, helpful, and has patience.
The teacher is kind, helpful, and patient.
The teacher is kind, being helpful, and patient.
The teacher is kind, helpful, and she has patience.
questions.explanation: All three items are adjectives (kind, helpful, patient), maintaining parallel structure.

title: Parts of Speech
description: Understanding the eight parts of speech in English
content:
The eight parts of speech are the building blocks of English sentences. Each word in a sentence functions as one of these parts, and understanding them helps you construct clear, grammatically correct sentences.

The Eight Parts of Speech:

  • Nouns: Person, place, thing, or idea (cat, Boston, happiness)
  • Pronouns: Replace nouns (he, she, it, they)
  • Verbs: Show action or state of being (run, is, think)
  • Adjectives: Describe nouns (blue, tall, amazing)
  • Adverbs: Describe verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs (quickly, very, well)
  • Prepositions: Show relationships between words (in, on, at, by)
  • Conjunctions: Connect words or groups of words (and, but, because)
  • Interjections: Express emotion (wow, ouch, hey)

Each part of speech has its own detailed topic for deeper study.

examples.label: Sentence with All Parts
examples.text: Wow! The quick brown fox (nouns/adjectives) jumps (verb) quickly (adverb) over the lazy dog, and (conjunction) it (pronoun) lands in (preposition) the garden.

examples.label: Identifying Parts
examples.text: She (pronoun) ran (verb) to (preposition) the (article) store (noun) quickly (adverb).

resources.title: Guide to Grammar: Parts of Speech

questions.question: What part of speech is the word 'quickly' in this sentence: 'She ran quickly.'
questions.explanation: 'Quickly' describes how she ran (modifies the verb), making it an adverb.

questions.question: What part of speech connects words or groups of words?
questions.explanation: Conjunctions connect words, phrases, or clauses (and, but, or, because).

questions.question: Which word is a pronoun?
questions.explanation: 'They' is a pronoun that replaces a noun.

questions.question: A word can only be one part of speech.
questions.explanation: False. Many words can function as different parts of speech depending on context (e.g., 'run' can be a noun or a verb).

title: Passive Voice
description: Understanding when and how to use passive voice
content:
In passive voice, the subject receives the action: 'The study was conducted by the researcher.' While active voice is often preferred, passive voice has legitimate uses in academic writing.

Use passive voice when: the action is more important than who did it, the doer is unknown or obvious, or you want to emphasize what was done rather than who did it. In scientific writing, passive voice is sometimes used to maintain objectivity.

examples.label: Appropriate Passive
examples.text: The samples were analyzed for contamination.

examples.label: Appropriate Passive
examples.text: Mistakes were made in the initial calculation.

examples.label: Better as Active
examples.text: The report was written by me. → I wrote the report.

resources.title: Purdue OWL: Active vs. Passive Voice

questions.question: Which sentence uses passive voice?
sentences: We submitted our work on time.
questions.explanation: 'The papers were graded overnight' is passive—the subject (papers) receives the action.

questions.question: Which is a good reason to use passive voice?
options: When you don't know who performed the action
questions.answer: When you don't know who performed the action
questions.explanation: Passive voice is appropriate when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or obvious from context.

title: Prepositional Phrases
description: Understanding and using prepositional phrases
content:
A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition (in, on, at, by, with, etc.) and ends with a noun or pronoun (the object of the preposition). These phrases add detail about time, location, direction, or other relationships.

Common prepositions: in, on, at, by, with, from, to, for, of, about, under, over, between, among, through, during, before, after.

examples.label: Location
examples.text: The book is on the table.

examples.label: Time
examples.text: We'll meet after class.

examples.label: Direction
examples.text: She walked toward the library.

examples.label: Multiple Phrases
examples.text: In the morning, I walk to school with my friend.

questions.question: Identify the prepositional phrase: 'The cat sat on the windowsill.'
questions.explanation: The prepositional phrase starts with the preposition 'on' and ends with the object 'windowsill.'

questions.question: A sentence can have more than one prepositional phrase.
questions.explanation: True. Sentences can contain multiple prepositional phrases, as in: 'In the morning, I walked through the park with my dog.'

title: Prepositions
description: Understanding prepositions: words that show relationships
content:
Prepositions show relationships between words in a sentence—typically relationships of place, time, or direction. A preposition is always followed by a noun or pronoun (the object of the preposition), forming a prepositional phrase.

Common Prepositions:

  • Place: in, on, at, under, over, between, among, behind, beside
  • Time: at, on, in, during, before, after, since, until
  • Direction: to, toward, from, into, onto, through
  • Other: with, without, about, for, of, by

For more detailed study of how prepositional phrases function in sentences, see our Prepositional Phrases topic.

examples.label: Place
examples.text: The book is on the table.

examples.label: Time
examples.text: We'll meet at noon.

examples.label: Direction
examples.text: She walked toward the library.

examples.label: Multiple Prepositions
examples.text: In the morning, I walked to school with my friend.

questions.question: Which word is a preposition?
questions.explanation: 'Under' is a preposition showing position or location.

questions.question: Identify the prepositional phrase: 'The cat sat on the mat.'
questions.explanation: 'On the mat' is the prepositional phrase (preposition + object).

questions.question: Which sentence contains a preposition?
questions.explanation: 'To' is a preposition in 'to school.'

questions.question: A preposition must always be followed by a noun or pronoun.
questions.explanation: True. Prepositions need an object (noun/pronoun) to form a prepositional phrase.

title: Pronoun Agreement
description: Making pronouns agree with their antecedents
content:
Pronouns must agree with their antecedents (the nouns they replace) in number and gender. Singular antecedents take singular pronouns; plural antecedents take plural pronouns.

Common issues: 1) Indefinite pronouns (everyone, somebody) are usually singular, 2) Company/organization names are usually singular, 3) Avoid unclear pronoun references.

examples.label: Correct
examples.text: Each student must bring their materials. (or: his or her materials)

examples.label: Incorrect
examples.text: Everyone should do what they want. (traditionally incorrect, but increasingly accepted)

examples.label: Correct
examples.text: The company announced its new policy.

examples.label: Unclear Reference
examples.text: John told Mark that he was wrong. (Who was wrong?)

examples.label: Clear
examples.text: John told Mark, "You were wrong."

questions.question: Which sentence has correct pronoun agreement?
options: Each of the students brought their lunch.
Each of the students brought his or her lunch.
Each of the students brought they lunch.
Each of the students brought its lunch.
questions.answer: Each of the students brought his or her lunch.
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular, so traditionally it takes singular pronouns. Note: 'their' is increasingly accepted in informal writing.

questions.question: The pronoun 'they' can only be used for plural antecedents.
questions.explanation: False. Singular 'they' is increasingly accepted in both informal and formal writing as a gender-neutral pronoun.

title: Pronouns
description: Understanding pronouns and pronoun case
content:
Pronouns replace nouns to avoid repetition. The form of a pronoun changes based on its function in the sentence.

Pronoun Case:

  • Subjective Case (subject of verb): I, you, he, she, it, we, they, who
  • Objective Case (object of verb/preposition): me, you, him, her, it, us, them, whom
  • Possessive Case (shows ownership): my, your, his, her, its, our, their, whose

Types of Pronouns:

  • Personal: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
  • Possessive: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs
  • Demonstrative: this, that, these, those
  • Relative: who, whom, which, that
  • Reflexive: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves

examples.label: Subjective Case
examples.text: She and I went to the store. (subjects)

examples.label: Objective Case
examples.text: The teacher called him and me. (objects of verb)

examples.label: After Preposition
examples.text: Between you and me, this is difficult. (objects of preposition)

examples.label: Common Error
examples.text: WRONG: Me and him went. CORRECT: He and I went.

questions.question: Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Use subjective case (she, I) when the pronoun is the subject of the verb.

questions.question: Which is correct: 'Between you and ___'?
questions.explanation: After a preposition (between), use objective case: 'Between you and me.'

questions.question: Which sentence uses pronouns correctly?
sentences: Me and John went to the park.
The gift is for he and I.
She gave it to him and me.
questions.explanation: 'Him and me' are both objective case, correct as objects of the preposition 'to.'

questions.question: You should always use 'I' instead of 'me.'
questions.explanation: False. Use 'I' for subjects and 'me' for objects. Both are correct in different contexts.

title: Quotation Marks
description: Using quotation marks correctly with direct quotes
content:
Quotation marks enclose direct quotes, dialogue, and titles of short works. In academic writing, they're most commonly used when incorporating source material.

Key rules: 1) Periods and commas go inside quotation marks, 2) Colons and semicolons go outside, 3) Use single quotes for quotes within quotes, 4) Introduce quotes with signal phrases.

examples.label: Direct Quote
examples.text: According to Smith, "Education is the key to success."

examples.label: Title of Short Work
examples.text: We read Poe's "The Tell-Tale Heart" in class.

examples.label: Dialogue
examples.text: She said, "I'll be there at noon."

examples.label: Quote within Quote
examples.text: The article states, "Critics call it 'revolutionary' in approach."

questions.question: Which sentence punctuates the quote correctly?
questions.explanation: The period goes inside the quotation marks, and there should be a comma before the quote begins.

questions.question: Periods always go inside quotation marks in American English.
questions.explanation: True. In American English, periods and commas always go inside closing quotation marks.

title: Run-on Sentences
description: Identifying and correcting run-on sentences
content:
A run-on sentence occurs when two or more independent clauses (complete sentences) are joined without proper punctuation or connecting words. There are two main types: fused sentences (no punctuation between clauses) and comma splices (only a comma between clauses).

Academic writing uses specific punctuation to show the relationship between ideas. This helps readers follow your thinking clearly.

examples.label: Run-on (Fused)
examples.text: I love reading it helps me relax.

examples.label: Corrected (Period)
examples.text: I love reading. It helps me relax.

examples.label: Run-on (Comma Splice)
examples.text: I love reading, it helps me relax.

examples.label: Corrected (Semicolon)
examples.text: I love reading; it helps me relax.

examples.label: Corrected (Conjunction)
examples.text: I love reading because it helps me relax.

resources.title: UNC Writing Center: Fragments and Run-ons

questions.question: Which sentence is a run-on?
sentences: The sun was setting, and the sky turned orange.
She studied hard she passed the exam.
After the rain stopped, we went outside.
questions.explanation: This is a fused sentence with two independent clauses joined without any punctuation or connecting word.

questions.question: Which is the best way to fix this run-on: 'It was cold outside, I wore a jacket'?
options: It was cold outside I wore a jacket.
It was cold outside, so I wore a jacket.
It was cold outside, I wore a jacket.
It was cold, outside I wore a jacket.
questions.answer: It was cold outside, so I wore a jacket.
questions.explanation: Adding a coordinating conjunction (so) after the comma properly connects the two independent clauses and shows the relationship between them.

questions.question: A comma by itself can join two independent clauses.
questions.explanation: False. Using only a comma to join independent clauses creates a comma splice, which is a type of run-on sentence. You need a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, or use a semicolon instead.

questions.question: Which punctuation mark can join two closely related independent clauses?
questions.explanation: A semicolon can join two independent clauses that are closely related in meaning.

title: Semicolons
description: Using semicolons to connect related ideas
content:
Semicolons connect two closely related independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction. They're stronger than a comma but not as final as a period.

Use semicolons when: 1) Joining related independent clauses, or 2) Separating items in a complex list (especially when items contain commas). Don't use semicolons to connect a dependent clause to an independent clause.

examples.label: Connecting Clauses
examples.text: She loves reading; her favorite genre is mystery.

examples.label: Complex List
examples.text: The team includes Ana, the designer; Marcus, the developer; and Joy, the project manager.

examples.label: Incorrect
examples.text: I was tired; because I stayed up late.

examples.label: Correct
examples.text: I was tired because I stayed up late.

resources.title: UNC Writing Center: Semicolons, Colons, and Commas

questions.question: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
options: I like pizza; but not pasta.
I like pizza; my sister prefers tacos.
I like pizza; because it's delicious.
questions.answer: I like pizza; my sister prefers tacos.
questions.explanation: Semicolons join two independent clauses that are closely related.

questions.question: You can use a semicolon before 'because.'
questions.explanation: False. 'Because' introduces a dependent clause, and semicolons should only join independent clauses.

title: Sentence Fragments
description: Understanding and fixing incomplete sentences
content:
A sentence fragment is an incomplete sentence that's missing a subject, a verb, or doesn't express a complete thought. While fragments are common in casual conversation, academic writing requires complete sentences.

Every complete sentence needs three things: a subject (who or what), a verb (action or state of being), and a complete thought that can stand alone.

Remember: In academic contexts, we use complete sentences to ensure clarity and precision. This doesn't mean other ways of communicating are incorrect—just that formal writing has specific conventions.

examples.label: Fragment
examples.text: Because I was tired.

examples.label: Complete
examples.text: I went to bed early because I was tired.

examples.label: Fragment
examples.text: Running through the park.

examples.label: Complete
examples.text: She was running through the park.

resources.title: UNC Writing Center: Fragments and Run-ons

questions.question: Which of the following is a sentence fragment?
sentences: The cat slept on the windowsill.
questions.explanation: 'After we finished dinner' is a dependent clause that cannot stand alone. It needs to be connected to an independent clause to form a complete sentence.

questions.question: How can you fix the fragment 'While walking to class'?
options: While walking to class, I saw my friend.
questions.answer: While walking to class, I saw my friend.
questions.explanation: Adding an independent clause ('I saw my friend') creates a complete sentence with both a dependent clause and an independent clause.

questions.question: A group of words must have both a subject and a verb to be a complete sentence.
questions.explanation: True. A complete sentence requires a subject, a verb, and must express a complete thought that can stand independently.

questions.question: Which sentence is complete?
questions.explanation: 'We went to the beach' has a subject (we), a verb (went), and expresses a complete thought.

questions.question: What makes 'Running quickly down the street' a fragment?
questions.explanation: While it has a verb form (running), there's no clear subject performing the action, making it incomplete.

title: Subject-Verb Agreement
description: Making subjects and verbs agree in number
content:
Subject-verb agreement means that singular subjects take singular verbs, and plural subjects take plural verbs. This is a standard convention in academic English that helps maintain clarity.

The basic rule: if your subject is singular (one person or thing), use a singular verb. If your subject is plural (more than one), use a plural verb. Watch out for tricky situations like words between the subject and verb, or indefinite pronouns.

examples.label: Correct (Singular)
examples.text: The student writes every day.

examples.label: Correct (Plural)
examples.text: The students write every day.

examples.label: Incorrect
examples.text: The student write every day.

examples.label: Tricky but Correct
examples.text: The box of chocolates is on the table.

questions.question: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
questions.explanation: 'Dogs' is plural, so it needs the plural verb 'bark' (not 'barks').

questions.question: Choose the correct verb: 'Everyone ____ ready for the test.'
questions.explanation: 'Everyone' is a singular indefinite pronoun, so it takes the singular verb 'is.'

questions.question: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
sentences: The list of items are on the desk.
The books on the shelf is dusty.
The children plays in the park.
questions.explanation: 'The professor teaches' is correct—singular subject with singular verb. The others have agreement errors.

title: That, Who, Which (Relative Pronouns)
description: Choosing the correct relative pronoun
content:
Relative pronouns connect clauses to nouns. The choice depends on whether you're referring to people or things, and whether the clause is essential (restrictive) or extra information (nonrestrictive).

Who: Use for people in both restrictive and nonrestrictive clauses.

That: Use for things in restrictive clauses (essential information, no commas). Can also be used for people in restrictive clauses, though 'who' is preferred.

Which: Use for things in nonrestrictive clauses (extra information, use commas). In American English, 'which' typically requires commas.

examples.label: People (Who)
examples.text: The student who studies hard will succeed.

examples.label: Things - Essential (That)
examples.text: The book that I borrowed is due tomorrow.

examples.label: Things - Extra Info (Which)
examples.text: The book, which I borrowed from the library, is excellent.

examples.label: People - Extra Info (Who)
examples.text: My sister, who lives in Boston, is visiting next week.

examples.label: Restrictive vs. Nonrestrictive
examples.text:
Dogs that bark loudly annoy neighbors. (only the loud ones)
Dogs, which are loyal animals, make great pets. (all dogs)

resources.title: UNC Writing Center: Commas with Clauses

questions.question: Which relative pronoun should you use for people?
questions.explanation: Both 'who' and 'that' can be used for people, though 'who' is generally preferred in formal writing.

questions.question: Complete: The car ___ I bought is very reliable.
questions.explanation: 'That' is correct for a restrictive clause about a thing (no commas needed for essential information).

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'which'?
sentences: The house which I want to buy is expensive.
People which live here are friendly.
The library, which opens at 9 AM, has many books.
The car which is red belongs to me.
questions.explanation: This correctly uses 'which' with commas for nonrestrictive (extra) information about a thing.

questions.question: 'Which' clauses should be set off with commas in American English.
questions.explanation: True. In American English, 'which' is typically used for nonrestrictive clauses that require commas.

title: Their, There, and They're
description: Distinguishing between three commonly confused words
content:
These three words sound the same but have completely different meanings and uses.

Their = possessive pronoun (belonging to them)
There = location or used with 'is/are'
They're = contraction meaning "they are"

Tip: Replace the word in your sentence. If "they are" fits, use they're. If you're talking about a place or using "is/are," use there. If you mean something belongs to them, use their.

examples.label: Their (Possessive)
examples.text: The students submitted their assignments.

examples.label: There (Location)
examples.text: Put the book over there.

examples.label: There (With is/are)
examples.text: There are three reasons for this decision.

examples.label: They're (Contraction)
examples.text: They're going to the library. (They are going)

resources.title: Guide to Grammar: There, Their, They're

questions.question: Choose the correct word: '___ going to the store.'
questions.explanation: Use 'they're' because it means 'they are.' 'They are going to the store' makes sense.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: '___ are several options available.'
questions.explanation: Use 'there' with 'are' to indicate existence or availability.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The team celebrated ___ victory.'
questions.explanation: Use 'their' because the victory belongs to the team (possessive).

questions.question: Which sentence is correct?
sentences: Their is a problem with this plan.
They're books are on the shelf.
There are many reasons to agree.
questions.explanation: 'There are many reasons' correctly uses 'there' with 'are.'

title: Thesis Statements
description: Writing clear, arguable thesis statements
content:
A thesis statement is the central claim or main point of your essay. It tells readers what you will argue and usually appears at the end of your introduction.

A strong thesis is specific, arguable, and focused. It's not just a fact or observation—it's a claim that you'll support with evidence. Think of it as a promise to your reader about what your essay will demonstrate.

examples.label: Weak (Too Broad)
examples.text: Social media affects society.

examples.label: Strong
examples.text: Social media platforms have fundamentally altered how young adults form and maintain relationships by prioritizing quantity of connections over quality of interaction.

examples.label: Weak (Just a Fact)
examples.text: Many students use laptops in class.

examples.label: Strong
examples.text: While laptops can be valuable learning tools, their unrestricted use in classrooms ultimately hinders student engagement and comprehension.

resources.title: Harvard Writing Center: Developing a Thesis

questions.question: Which is the strongest thesis statement?
sentences: This paper is about climate change.
Governments must implement carbon pricing to effectively reduce emissions and combat climate change.
questions.explanation: This thesis is specific, arguable, and makes a clear claim that can be supported with evidence.

questions.question: A thesis statement should always be a fact that everyone agrees with.
questions.explanation: False. A thesis should be arguable—something you need to prove with evidence, not a simple fact.

questions.question: Where does the thesis statement typically appear?
options: At the end of the introduction
In the first sentence of the essay
questions.answer: At the end of the introduction
questions.explanation: The thesis statement typically appears at the end of the introductory paragraph, after you've provided context for your argument.

title: Thesis Statements for Literary Analysis
description: Writing effective thesis statements for literature essays
content:
A literary analysis thesis makes an arguable claim about how a text creates meaning through literary elements like character, symbolism, theme, structure, or language.

A strong literary thesis:
- Makes a specific, arguable interpretation
- Identifies the literary work and author
- Focuses on HOW the text achieves its effects
- Goes beyond plot summary
- Can be supported with textual evidence

examples.label: Weak (Plot Summary)
examples.text: In 'The Great Gatsby,' Gatsby loves Daisy and dies at the end.

examples.label: Strong (Analysis)
examples.text: Through Gatsby's elaborate parties and symbolic green light, Fitzgerald critiques the hollowness of the American Dream in 1920s society.

examples.label: Weak (Too Obvious)
examples.text: Shakespeare's 'Hamlet' is about revenge.

examples.label: Strong (Arguable)
examples.text: In 'Hamlet,' Shakespeare uses the play-within-a-play to explore how performance and deception blur the boundaries between reality and illusion.

questions.question: Which is a strong literary analysis thesis?
sentences: In 'The Yellow Wallpaper,' the narrator goes crazy.
Charlotte Perkins Gilman wrote 'The Yellow Wallpaper' in 1892.
'The Yellow Wallpaper' is a great short story that everyone should read.
Through the symbol of the wallpaper, Gilman exposes how 19th-century medical practices oppressed women's autonomy and mental health.
questions.explanation: This thesis makes an arguable claim about HOW Gilman uses a literary element (symbolism) to convey meaning.

questions.question: A good literary thesis should focus on plot summary.
questions.explanation: False. Literary thesis statements analyze HOW the text creates meaning, not just WHAT happens in the plot.

questions.question: What makes a literary thesis arguable?
options: It makes an interpretation that requires textual evidence to support
It mentions the title and author
questions.answer: It makes an interpretation that requires textual evidence to support
questions.explanation: An arguable thesis presents an interpretation that isn't obvious and must be proven with evidence from the text.

title: Topic Sentences
description: Crafting effective topic sentences for paragraphs
content:
A topic sentence states the main idea of a paragraph. It usually appears at the beginning and tells readers what the paragraph will discuss.

Think of topic sentences as mini-thesis statements for each paragraph. They should connect back to your thesis while introducing the specific point this paragraph will make. Good topic sentences help readers follow your argument.

examples.label: Weak
examples.text: There are many reasons for this.

examples.label: Strong
examples.text: The economic impact of remote work has been particularly significant in urban housing markets.

examples.label: Weak
examples.text: Another thing to consider is education.

examples.label: Strong
examples.text: Educational inequality begins long before students enter college, with underfunded K-12 schools creating persistent achievement gaps.

resources.title: Purdue OWL: Paragraphs and Topic Sentences

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a topic sentence?
options: To state the main idea of the paragraph
questions.answer: To state the main idea of the paragraph
questions.explanation: A topic sentence introduces the main idea that the paragraph will develop and support.

questions.question: Every paragraph should have a topic sentence.
questions.explanation: True. Topic sentences help organize your writing and guide readers through your argument.

title: Transitions
description: Using transitional words and phrases effectively
content:
Transitions are words or phrases that connect ideas and help your writing flow smoothly. They show relationships between sentences and paragraphs, guiding readers through your argument.

Common types: 1) Addition (furthermore, moreover, additionally), 2) Contrast (however, nevertheless, on the other hand), 3) Cause/Effect (therefore, consequently, as a result), 4) Time (meanwhile, subsequently, finally), 5) Example (for instance, specifically, to illustrate).

examples.label: Addition
examples.text: The study found significant results. Moreover, these results were replicated in later research.

examples.label: Contrast
examples.text: Many expected the proposal to fail. However, it passed with overwhelming support.

examples.label: Cause/Effect
examples.text: The experiment was flawed. Consequently, the results cannot be trusted.

examples.label: Example
examples.text: Several factors contributed to the outcome. For instance, funding played a crucial role.

questions.question: Which transition word shows contrast?
questions.explanation: 'However' signals a contrast or difference from the previous idea.

questions.question: Which transition would best show cause and effect?
questions.explanation: 'Consequently' shows that something happened as a result of what came before.

title: Using Quotes in Literary Analysis
description: Effectively integrating quotations from literature into your analysis
content:
In literary analysis, quotes from the text serve as evidence for your arguments. Integrate them smoothly into your writing, analyze them, and always explain their significance.

Key principles:
- Introduce quotes with signal phrases
- Keep quotes relatively brief
- Follow quotes with analysis—never leave them standing alone
- Use quotes to support your point, not make it for you
- Cite page numbers or line numbers

examples.label: Quote Sandwich (Good)
examples.text: The narrator's isolation is evident in her description of the wallpaper. She states, "The color is repellant, almost revolting; a smouldering unclean yellow" (Gilman 3). This visceral language reveals her deteriorating mental state, as she projects her feelings onto her surroundings.

examples.label: Dropped Quote (Bad)
examples.text: The narrator is isolated. "The color is repellant, almost revolting; a smouldering unclean yellow." She is going crazy.

examples.label: Good Integration
examples.text: Fitzgerald describes Gatsby's smile as one that "understood you just as far as you wanted to be understood" (48), suggesting his ability to manipulate others' perceptions.

resources.title: Purdue OWL: Quoting, Paraphrasing, and Summarizing

questions.question: You should always explain the significance of a quote after including it.
questions.explanation: True. Never leave a quote standing alone—always analyze it and explain how it supports your argument.

questions.question: What is a 'dropped quote'?
options: A quote with no introduction or analysis
A quote from a minor character
questions.answer: A quote with no introduction or analysis
questions.explanation: A dropped quote appears without introduction or follow-up analysis, making it seem disconnected from your argument.
