questions.question: Which demonstrates good quote integration?
sentences: "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times." This shows contrast.
Dickens uses parallelism. "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times."
Dickens opens with a paradox, stating "it was the best of times, it was the worst of times" (1), establishing the novel's theme of duality.
"It was the best of times, it was the worst of times." Dickens wrote this.
questions.explanation: This introduces the quote, integrates it smoothly, cites it, and explains its significance.

title: Verbs
description: Understanding verbs: action, state of being, tense, and types
content:
Verbs express action or state of being. Every complete sentence needs a verb.

Types of Verbs:

  • Action Verbs: Show physical or mental action (run, think, write)
  • Linking Verbs: Connect subject to description (is, am, are, was, were, become, seem)
  • Helping Verbs: Assist main verb (will, can, should, have, has, had)
  • Transitive Verbs: Take a direct object (She kicked the ball.)
  • Intransitive Verbs: No direct object (He sleeps.)

Verb Tense:

  • Present: I walk, she walks
  • Past: I walked, she walked
  • Future: I will walk, she will walk
  • Present Perfect: I have walked
  • Past Perfect: I had walked
  • Future Perfect: I will have walked

Conjugation is changing the verb form to match the subject and tense.

examples.label: Transitive (needs object)
examples.text: She threw the ball. (What did she throw? The ball.)

examples.label: Intransitive (no object)
examples.text: The baby cried. (Cried what? Nothing—intransitive.)

examples.label: Tense Change
examples.text: I walk (present), I walked (past), I will walk (future)

examples.label: Conjugation
examples.text: I am, you are, he/she/it is, we are, they are

resources.title: Schoolhouse Rock: Verb - That's What's Happening

questions.question: Which verb is transitive?
questions.explanation: 'Ate' is transitive because it takes a direct object (pizza). The others are intransitive.

questions.question: What tense is 'will have finished'?
questions.explanation: 'Will have finished' is future perfect—an action that will be completed before a future time.

questions.question: Which is a linking verb?
questions.explanation: 'Seems' is a linking verb that connects the subject to a description.

questions.question: All verbs take a direct object.
questions.explanation: False. Only transitive verbs take direct objects. Intransitive verbs do not.

title: Who vs. Whom
description: Understanding when to use 'who' and 'whom'
content:
The difference between 'who' and 'whom' is based on grammatical function. Use 'who' when it's the subject of a verb (the one doing the action). Use 'whom' when it's the object of a verb or preposition (the one receiving the action).

A simple trick: If you can replace it with 'he' or 'she,' use 'who.' If you can replace it with 'him' or 'her,' use 'whom.'

Note: In informal speech and writing, 'who' is increasingly used in all positions, but formal academic writing still observes the who/whom distinction.

examples.label: Subject (Who)
examples.text: Who ate the last cookie? (He ate it.)

examples.label: Object (Whom)
examples.text: To whom did you give the book? (You gave it to him.)

examples.label: Subject (Who)
examples.text: The student who studied hard passed the exam.

examples.label: Object (Whom)
examples.text: The professor whom I respect most is retiring.

examples.label: After Preposition (Whom)
examples.text: With whom are you going to the concert? (You're going with her.)

questions.question: Which is correct?
questions.explanation: In formal writing, 'whom' is correct because it's the object of the verb 'call' (You called him/her).

questions.question: Complete: The woman ___ lives next door is a doctor.
questions.explanation: 'Who' is correct because it's the subject of 'lives' (She lives next door).

questions.question: Which sentence uses 'whom' correctly?
sentences: The person whom called is waiting.
She is someone whom I admire greatly.
questions.explanation: 'Whom' is correct here because it's the object of the verb 'admire' (I admire her).

questions.question: After a preposition (to, for, with), you should use 'whom.'
questions.explanation: True. Pronouns that follow prepositions are objects, so 'whom' is correct: 'To whom did you speak?'

title: Wordiness and Clarity
description: Eliminating unnecessary words and writing with clarity
content:
Clear, concise writing communicates ideas efficiently without sacrificing meaning. Wordiness occurs when writers use more words than necessary, which can obscure meaning and frustrate readers. Academic writing values precision and clarity.

Common causes of wordiness: redundant phrases ('past history,' 'future plans'), weak verb constructions ('make a decision' instead of 'decide'), excessive prepositional phrases, and unnecessary qualifiers ('very,' 'really').

To improve clarity: Choose strong, specific verbs; eliminate redundancy; avoid empty phrases; get to the point quickly.

examples.label: Wordy
examples.text: In my personal opinion, I believe that the use of cell phones while driving is a dangerous activity that should be avoided at all times.

examples.label: Clear and Concise
examples.text: Using cell phones while driving is dangerous and should be avoided.

examples.label: Wordy
examples.text: The reason why the experiment failed is due to the fact that the temperature was not maintained at the proper level.

examples.label: Clear and Concise
examples.text: The experiment failed because the temperature was not properly maintained.

examples.label: Redundant
examples.text: She repeated the same experiment again.

examples.label: Concise
examples.text: She repeated the experiment.

questions.question: Which sentence is most concise?
options: Due to the fact that it was raining, we decided to cancel the picnic.
Because of the rain, we cancelled the picnic.
The picnic was cancelled by us because it was raining.
It was raining, so the decision was made to cancel the picnic.
questions.answer: Because of the rain, we cancelled the picnic.
questions.explanation: This version eliminates wordy phrases like 'due to the fact that' and uses active voice.

questions.question: Which phrase is redundant?
questions.explanation: 'Final outcome' is redundant because 'outcome' already implies finality.

questions.question: Which revision removes unnecessary words?
options: In the event that you are late, please call.
If you are going to be late, please call.
Should you be late, a call would be appreciated.
questions.explanation: This version is the most concise while maintaining the complete meaning.

questions.question: Writing concisely means making every sentence as short as possible.
questions.explanation: False. Concise writing means eliminating unnecessary words while preserving meaning and clarity, not just making sentences shorter.
